title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
claim: Writing episode lessons directly into memory causes overgeneralization and forgetting; testing them as hypotheses in a temporary state commits only verified updates.
layout: Left episode flow feeds two right panels: prior (top) versus ours (bottom), arrows throughout
description: The figure has three rounded panels. On the left, an agent episode runs top to bottom: a user task (book a round-trip NYC to SFO flight), agent interaction in a mock browser flight form, and environment feedback (booking confirmed). It ends in a 'Candidate lesson' box. Two black arrows send the lesson to the right. The top-right red panel, 'Prior: Direct memory writing', shows a Memory Bank database. It points to a green 'Helps similar tasks' box and red boxes labeled 'Boundary case overgeneralization' and 'Regression on archived skills (forgetting)'. The bottom-right blue panel, 'Ours: Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution', shows a structured hypothesis of four icons: precondition, behavior, effect and verifier. It flows to a temporary state, then to Transfer, Falsification and Regression probes, then a Gate. The gate leads to Commit, Refine or Reject icons. Red marks the prior approach and blue marks ours.
caption: A locally useful episode-derived lesson may overgeneralize or regress archived skills if directly written into memory. FGSE tests each lesson as a structured hypothesis in a temporary state and commits only verified, transferable updates to long-term memory.
abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $Ï$-Retail/$Ï$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.
